segments.caption: How can a poll of just 1,000 people predict an election?
The Central Limit Theorem. One example in detail, then 4 more places it's used. Save this one!
Millions of people will vote. A pollster can't ask them all, so they ask 1,000 random voters.
Each person gives one answer: yes or no. As data, that's just two bars. Nothing like a bell curve.
Now count the yeses: 520 out of 1,000. That's 52%.
And here's the key. Every yes is a 1, every no is a 0. 52% is just their average.
Now imagine running the same poll again and again, each time with a different 1,000 people.
You'd get 51, then 53, 52, 50, 54. Stack all those results, and they form a bell curve.
Most results land close to the middle. Only a few land far away.
That's the Central Limit Theorem: averages form a bell, even when each answer is just yes or no.
How wide is that bell? Its spread, the standard error, is the square root of p times 1 - p, over n.
0.52 × 0.48, over 1,000, square-rooted: about 1.6%.
In a bell, 95% of results land within about 2 standard errors. 2 × 1.6: about 3%.
So the pollster can say: 52%, ±3%. The true support is probably between 49 and 55.
That range, 49 to 55, is the margin of error, also called a 95% confidence interval.
Without the Central Limit Theorem, there would be no plus or minus at all.
Want a smaller margin? Ask 4 times as many people. 4,000 voters halves it, to ±1.5%.
Similarly, the Central Limit Theorem is used in:
A/B tests: the average spend per user, compared between two versions.
Factories: the average weight of 5 bottles, checked every hour.
Insurance: the average claim of thousands of customers, used to set premiums.
And machine learning: test accuracy, which is an average of right and wrong predictions.
Same idea every time: single values can be messy, but averages form a bell, and the bell tells you how sure to be.
